newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Minister admits Czech capital market works badly.
newsitem.headline: Minister admits Czech capital market works badly.

text.p: The Czech capital markets do not function properly and the situation can put off foreign investors, Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy told a news conference on Friday.
"I absolutely agree with you, you can put this on the record," Dlouhy said in response to a jouranlist's remark that the Czech capital market does not work properly at all.

"The credibility (of the Czech Republic) is also provided by the situation on capital market. The negative situation on the capital market may have a negative influence on foreign investors," Dlouhy said.
Investors have repeatedly complained about how opaque the Czech capital markets are and have questioned the resolve of the finance ministry to improve the trading environment.
Numerous foreign investors have cited poor legislation and regulation of information and ownership structures as reasons for diverting investment to other markets in the region.

Czech media have been awash recently with stories about how foreign portfolio investment is increasingly avoiding the country, and putting pressure on the government to do something to improve the situation.
"I do not remember, that (capital market reform) was on the agenda of the governmnet in the last weeks," the minister said.

Equities analysts have called for a securities commission staffed by top specialists and given ample powers to regulate the capital markets, instead of the finance ministry department which they say is underfunded and understaffed.
Prague Stock Exchange Chairman Tomas Jezek has been leading a move to establish a U.S.-style Securities and Exchange Commission funded by a fee on each transaction.

But this would need approval from a government which has yet to say whethter it would support the plan, and from parliament. Jezek has said that this commission could not possibly begin to function before the middle of next year.
